claims.text: The initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneous and equimolar, with a uniform elemental distribution.
Thermal exposure causes Cu to preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituent elements.
Cu enrichment reduces the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
The reduction in local melting temperature nucleates localized surface premelting.
Localized surface melting propagates inward and governs the progression toward complete melting.
The inward progression of melting occurs through defect nucleation and enhanced diffusion.
Melting will begin at surface regions exhibiting Cu enrichment.
Cu-rich surface regions will begin localized melting at a lower temperature than the homogeneous baseline.
Artificial enhancement of surface Cu concentration will advance the melting onset relative to homogeneous samples.
Following surface melting, a melt front will propagate from the surface toward the nanoparticle interior.
The proposed comparison uses identically heated nanoparticles initialized either homogeneously or with artificially enhanced Cu surface concentration.
The proposed boundary conditions are vacuum, uniform particle size, and no external stress or forces.
The mechanism is expected to apply when particles are small enough for surface effects to dominate but large enough not to be entirely governed by finite-size effects.
Homogeneous baseline nanoparticles do not exhibit premature surface melting below the alloy bulk melting temperature.

contradictions.description: The tested particles and the baseline are both described as initially homogeneous, but the hypothesis predicts thermally induced Cu segregation and premature surface melting in the initially homogeneous particles while the baseline stipulates that homogeneous particles do not exhibit such melting. The distinguishing control condition is therefore not consistently defined.
